lessons.title: Feeding the Dry Sow
lessons.body: A dry sow is a sow that is not pregnant and not lactating. She still needs good care to get back into condition for the next breeding. Feed her a maintenance diet of about 2 kg per day of a good sow ration. This ration should have 14% protein and be high in fibre, like maize bran or wheat bran. If she is too thin, increase to 2.5 kg; if too fat, reduce to 1.5 kg. Always provide plenty of clean waterâat least 10 litres per day. In hot African climates, sows may eat less, so feed early morning and late evening when it is cooler. Group-housed dry sows need space to avoid bullying; give each sow at least 2 square metres. If you keep them in individual stalls, make sure they can lie down and stand up comfortably. Watch for signs of heat (oestrus) every dayâa dry sow that is not cycling may need a boar nearby or a change in feed. Flushing (increasing feed to 3 kg per day) for 10-14 days before mating can increase ovulation rate. But do not overfeed, as fat sows have difficult births. Keep a record of each sow's feed and body condition. In Africa, many farmers use local feeds like sweet potato vines, cassava leaves, and kitchen waste, but these must be balanced with a commercial or home-mixed concentrate. A simple home mix: 50% maize, 20% bran, 20% protein concentrate (like soy or fish meal), 10% minerals and salt. Always store feed in a dry place to prevent mould. A dry sow that is well managed will give you many healthy litters.

lessons.title: Feeding the Pregnant Sow
lessons.body: Once a sow is confirmed pregnant, her feeding changes. For the first 80 days of pregnancy, feed her about 2 kg per day of a 14% protein sow ration. Do not overfeed, because too much energy can cause the embryos to die. From day 80 to farrowing (about 114 days), increase to 2.5-3 kg per day. This is when the piglets grow fast and the sow needs extra nutrients. Use a ration with 16% protein and added calcium and phosphorus for strong bones. Provide 15-20 litres of water daily. In the last week before farrowing, reduce feed slightly to 2 kg and add bran to prevent constipation. A pregnant sow should have a body condition score of 3 out of 5ânot too thin, not too fat. Check her udder: it should start to develop and may leak milk a few days before birth. Keep her in a clean, quiet pen away from other sows. In Africa, many farmers use group housing for pregnant sows, but individual pens are better to prevent fighting and ensure each sow gets her share. If you use local feeds, make sure they are not mouldyâmouldy feed can cause abortion. Add a mineral supplement if your soil is deficient in selenium or zinc. Weigh feed with a simple scale or use a tin can as a measure (a standard 2-litre tin holds about 1.5 kg of maize). Record feed intake daily. A sow that is too thin will have small piglets; a sow that is too fat will have difficulty farrowing. Adjust feed based on her condition. Always consult a vet if you see signs of illness. Good feeding during pregnancy means strong, healthy piglets and a sow that recovers quickly after birth.

lessons.title: Feeding the Lactating Sow
lessons.body: A lactating sow is feeding piglets, so she needs a lot of energy and protein. Feed her free-choice, meaning she can eat as much as she wants, but start slowly after farrowing. On day 1 after birth, give only 1 kg of feed. Increase by 0.5 kg each day until she is eating 2 kg plus 0.5 kg for each piglet she is nursing. For example, a sow with 10 piglets should eat 2 + (10 x 0.5) = 7 kg per day. Use a high-energy, 18% protein lactation ration. Provide unlimited clean waterâshe may drink 20-30 litres daily. If she does not eat enough, she will lose body condition and produce less milk. In Africa, you can supplement with local feeds like cooked sweet potato, pumpkin, or milk from cattle, but always include a balanced concentrate. Feed her 2-3 times a day, and remove any leftover feed to prevent spoilage. Keep the farrowing pen coolâuse shade, ventilation, or wet the floor. A hot sow will eat less. Watch her udder for mastitis (hard, hot, painful). If she has mastitis, she may refuse to feed piglets. Consult a vet. Also, ensure piglets have access to creep feed from 2 weeks old to reduce demand on the sow. Weigh the sow weekly or use body condition scoring. If she is losing too much weight, increase feed. If she is too fat, reduce slightly. After weaning, reduce feed to 2 kg per day to help her dry off. Good lactation feeding means heavy piglets and a sow that returns to heat quickly. Remember, a sow that is well fed will produce 20-30 piglets per year. Poor feeding means fewer, smaller piglets and longer time to rebreed.

lessons.title: Body Condition Scoring
lessons.body: Body condition scoring (BCS) is a simple way to check if your sow is too thin, too fat, or just right. Use a scale of 1 to 5, where 1 is very thin and 5 is very fat. A score of 3 is ideal. To score, look at the sow from the side and behind. Feel her backbone, ribs, and hip bones. If you can easily feel the bones with light pressure, she is thin (score 2). If you cannot feel them even with firm pressure, she is fat (score 4 or 5). If you can feel them with firm pressure but not see them, she is ideal (score 3). Also check the tailhead and pin bones. In Africa, where feed can be scarce, many sows are too thin. A thin sow will have weak piglets and poor milk. A fat sow will have difficulty giving birth and may crush piglets. Score your sows every month. Keep a record for each sow. If a sow scores 2, increase her feed by 0.5-1 kg per day. If she scores 4, reduce feed by 0.5 kg and increase exercise. For pregnant sows, aim for score 3 at mating, then maintain until day 80, then allow slight increase. For lactating sows, they will naturally lose condition; aim to have them at score 3 when weaned. Use a simple chart with pictures to help you. You can draw the scores on a paper or use a notebook. In group housing, score each sow individually because dominant sows may eat more. If you cannot feel the bones, use a measuring tape to check girth. A sow with a girth of more than 1.5 metres may be too fat. Body condition scoring is free and takes only a few minutes. It helps you adjust feeding and prevent problems. Train your workers to do it. Good BCS means healthy sows and more profit.

lessons.title: Culling Old Sows
lessons.body: Culling means removing a sow from the breeding herd. You cull old sows when they are no longer productive. Most sows stay productive for 6-8 litters, or until they are 4-5 years old. Signs it is time to cull: she has fewer than 8 piglets per litter, she has difficulty farrowing, she has poor milk, she has lost body condition and does not recover, she has repeated health problems like mastitis or lameness, or she is aggressive and injures other sows. Also cull if she fails to conceive after two matings. In Africa, where feed is expensive, keeping a low-producing sow wastes money. A good sow should wean at least 20 piglets per year. If she weans fewer than 16, consider culling. To cull, first confirm she is not pregnant. Sell her to a butcher or another farmer. In some areas, you can sell cull sows for meatâthey are often used for sausages or minced meat. Before selling, check local regulations and ensure she is healthy. Do not sell a sow with disease. If you cannot sell, you may slaughter for home consumption. After culling, replace her with a gilt (young female pig) that you have raised or bought. Keep records of each sow's performance: number of piglets born alive, weaned, and weaning weight. Use a notebook or a simple spreadsheet. This helps you decide which sows to keep. Culling is not failureâit is good management. It keeps your herd productive and profitable. Plan to cull 20-25% of your sows each year. This means if you have 10 sows, replace 2-3 each year. Always have replacement gilts ready. In batch farrowing, culling must be done between batches to avoid disruption. A well-culled herd has healthy, productive sows that give you daily pig sales.

lessons.title: Managing the Boar
lessons.body: A boar is a male pig used for breeding. A good boar is calm, has strong legs, and comes from a healthy line. Keep one boar for every 10-15 sows. In Africa, many farmers cannot afford artificial insemination, so a boar is essential. Feed your boar a special boar ration with 14% protein. Give him 2-2.5 kg per day. If he is used for mating often, increase to 3 kg. Do not overfeed, as fat boars have poor libido and difficulty mating. Provide plenty of water and exercise. A boar needs spaceâat least 6 square metres. If he is tethered, give him a chain and a comfortable pen. Boars can be aggressive, so handle them calmly and never turn your back. Use a pig board (a flat board) to move him safely. Check his feet and legs regularly; lame boars cannot mate. Trim his tusks if they grow too long. A boar can mate from 8 months old, but wait until he is 10-12 months for heavy use. Use him for at most 2 matings per week when young, and up to 4-5 per week when mature. Always bring the sow to the boar's pen for matingâthis reduces fighting. Mating takes 5-10 minutes. If the boar is not interested, check for heat in the sow or health problems in the boar. In hot climates, boars may be less fertile; provide shade and cool water. Rotate boars every 2 years to prevent inbreeding. If you have only one boar, replace him after 2 years with a new one from a different farm. Keep records of each mating: date, sow, and boar. This helps you predict farrowing dates. A well-managed boar will give you many healthy litters. Remember, a boar is half your herd's genetics, so take good care of him.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sow and Boar Feeding & Management Benchmarks for African Pig Enterprises

This practical reference consolidates the feeding and management decisions that determine whether a batch-farrowing pig unit in Africa makes money or loses it. In a batch system, every sow is either dry, pregnant, or lactating at a predictable time â so feed, labour, and housing can be planned like a factory production line. The financial logic is simple: a sow that weans 10â11 strong piglets per litter, twice a year, at low feed cost per piglet weaned, is profitable. A sow that weans 6 piglets after eating 1.2 tonnes of feed per year is a loss-making asset that should have been culled three parities ago.

Use the figures below as working benchmarks, not gospel. Adjust to your own feed prices, local maize and soya availability, and market weights (many African markets prefer 60â80 kg live weight "porkers" rather than 100â110 kg). Track your own numbers for at least three parities before making big culling decisions.

Feeding the Dry Sow

The dry period is short â typically 5â7 days from weaning to service. The goal is to flush the sow so she ovulates more eggs, then get her served promptly. Feed a maintenance-plus ration of 2.0â2.5 kg/day of a sow diet containing 13â14% crude protein (CP). In the 3â5 days before service, "flushing" with an extra 0.5â1.0 kg/day can raise ovulation rate, especially in thin sows (BCS 2). Do not over-flush fat sows â they have more difficulty conceiving. Ensure continuous access to clean water and a mineral premix, particularly in areas where soil is selenium- or zinc-deficient (common in parts of East and Southern Africa).

Feeding the Pregnant Sow

Gestation is 114 days (range 112â116). The critical rule: do not overfeed the pregnant sow. Overfeeding causes fat sows, difficult farrowing, low milk yield, and crushed piglets. Feed 2.2â2.8 kg/day of a 14â15% CP gestation diet, split into two meals. The first 80 days is maintenance only; the last 30 days is when 60% of foetal growth occurs, so increase carefully to 2.8â3.0 kg/day in the final three weeks, especially for thin sows. Use a simple body condition score (see below) to fine-tune.

Table 1: Daily feed allowance by phase (75 kg mature sow, tropical climate)
Phase Days Feed (kg/day) Crude Protein Notes
Dry / weaned5â72.0â2.513â14%Flush 3â5 days pre-service
Early gestation (day 0â80)802.2â2.514%Maintenance only
Late gestation (day 81â114)342.6â3.015%Foetal growth surge
Lactation (first 7 days)74.0â5.016â18%Ramp up gradually
Lactation (days 8â28)215.5â6.516â18%Feed to appetite + 0.4 kg/piglet
Boar (working)â2.5â3.014%Reduce 2 weeks before service

Source: Adapted from FAO (2012), Pig Sector Development in Africa; ILRI smallholder pig production guidelines; and NRC (2012), Nutrient Requirements of Swine.

Feeding the Lactating Sow

Lactation is where money is made or lost. A sow suckling 10 piglets produces 6â8 litres of milk per day and needs 5.5â6.5 kg of a 16â18% CP diet daily. The simple rule of thumb used across African extension services: 2 kg maintenance + 0.4 kg per suckling piglet. A sow with 10 piglets needs about 6 kg/day. Feed to appetite â do not restrict. If the sow loses more than 10 kg during lactation, she will take longer to return to heat and will wean fewer piglets in the next litter. Provide unlimited clean water; a lactating sow drinks 20â30 litres per day. In hot climates, feed in the cool of early morning and evening to boost intake.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Aflatoxin and Mouldy Feed

Never feed sows maize or groundnut cake that is mouldy, musty, or discoloured. Aflatoxin B1 â common in poorly stored African maize and groundnuts â causes liver damage, abortions, stillbirths, and low milk yield. It also passes into pork, creating a human food safety risk. Store feed on pallets in a dry, ventilated room, use within 4 weeks, and never feed damp or heated feed. If you suspect aflatoxin, discard the batch; do not "dilute" it with good feed. Wear gloves and a dust mask when handling suspect feed.

Body Condition Scoring (BCS)

BCS is the single most useful management tool for a sow herd. Score each sow at weaning, at service, at day 60 of gestation, and at farrowing. Use a 1â5 scale by feeling the backbone, ribs, and hip bones. Target BCS 3 (ribs not seen but easily felt; hip bones rounded).

Table 2: Body Condition Score (BCS 1â5) and management action
BCS Description Action
1Very thin â ribs, spine, hips sharpIncrease feed 0.5â1.0 kg/day; check for worms and disease; do not serve until BCS 3
2Thin â bones easily feltIncrease feed 0.3â0.5 kg/day; flush before service
3Ideal â ribs felt but not seenMaintain current ration; the target for all sows
4Fat â ribs hard to feelReduce feed 0.3â0.5 kg/day; risk of farrowing problems
5Very fat â ribs not feltReduce feed 0.5â1.0 kg/day; cull if repeatedly BCS 5

Source: Adapted from BPEX/ AHDB (UK) Pork Body Condition Scoring guidelines and FAO smallholder pig extension materials.

Culling Old Sows

Culling is a business decision, not an emotional one. Keep a sow only while she earns her keep. Cull when:

  • She has weaned fewer than 7 piglets in two consecutive litters.
  • She has failed to conceive after two services (repeat breeder).
  • She has had two consecutive difficult farrowings or a prolapse.
  • She is BCS 1 or BCS 5 at weaning and does not recover.
  • She has poor udders, mastitis history, or has crushed piglets more than once.
  • She has reached parity 7â8 (in most African herds, cull at parity 6â7).

Replace culled sows with home-bred or purchased gilts so that 20â25% of the breeding herd is replaced each year. In batch systems, plan replacements to enter the batch at the same time as the rest of the group.

Managing the Boar

A working boar is expensive to keep and easy to ruin. Feed a 14% CP ration at 2.5â3.0 kg/day, but reduce to 2.0â2.5 kg/day for two weeks before heavy service to keep him active. Boars need exercise â walk them daily. Keep them cool; heat stress above 30Â°C reduces sperm quality for 4â6 weeks. Use one boar for no more than 2 services per week when young (under 12 months) and up to 4â5 per week when mature. Rotate boars every 12â18 months to avoid inbreeding. In African conditions with limited AI access, a healthy boar is a critical asset â treat him like the most valuable animal on the farm.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Weigh or measure feed daily â do not estimate by eye.
  2. Score every sow at weaning, service, day 60, and farrowing; target BCS 3.
  3. Lactating sows: 2 kg + 0.4 kg per piglet per day, fed to appetite.
  4. Clean, cool water available 24/7 â 20â30 litres/day for lactating sows.
  5. Store feed dry, on pallets, use within 4 weeks; reject any mouldy batch.
  6. Deworm sows before service and treat for mange and lice.
  7. Cull any sow that weans fewer than 7 piglets in two consecutive litters.
  8. Replace 20â25% of the breeding herd each year with healthy gilts.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Pig Sector Development in Africa (PDF)
  • FAO â Good Practices for the Feed Sector (2020)
  • ILRI â Smallholder Pig Production and Marketing in Africa
  • WOAH â Terrestrial Animal Health Code (pig welfare and feeding)
  • AHDB â Body Condition Scoring of Sows (free guide)

Prepared for the Rise AFRICA Skills course Daily Pig Sales: Batch Farrowing System. Benchmarks are indicative; always validate against local feed analyses, market prices, and veterinary advice.

quiz.q: How much feed per day is recommended for a dry sow?
quiz.explanation: A dry sow needs about 2 kg of a maintenance diet per day.

quiz.q: What is the ideal body condition score for a sow?
quiz.explanation: A score of 3 out of 5 is idealânot too thin, not too fat.

quiz.q: What should you do if a dry sow is too thin?
quiz.explanation: Increase feed to 2.5 kg per day to help her gain condition.

quiz.q: How many litres of water does a dry sow need daily?
quiz.explanation: A dry sow needs at least 10 litres of clean water per day.

quiz.q: What is flushing in pig farming?
options: A) Giving extra feed before mating
quiz.explanation: Flushing means increasing feed for 10-14 days before mating to boost ovulation.

quiz.q: During early pregnancy (first 80 days), how much feed should a sow get?
quiz.explanation: About 2 kg per day is enough to maintain pregnancy without overfeeding.

quiz.q: What protein level is recommended for a pregnant sow in late gestation?
quiz.explanation: A 16% protein ration supports fetal growth and udder development.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mouldy feed for pregnant sows?
quiz.explanation: Mouldy feed can contain toxins that cause abortion.

quiz.q: What should you do in the last week before farrowing?
options: B) Reduce feed slightly and add bran
quiz.explanation: Reducing feed and adding bran prevents constipation and reduces farrowing problems.

quiz.q: How much feed should a lactating sow get on day 1 after farrowing?
quiz.explanation: Start with 1 kg on day 1 and gradually increase.

quiz.q: How much extra feed per piglet nursing should a lactating sow receive?
quiz.explanation: For each piglet, add 0.5 kg to the base 2 kg.

quiz.q: What protein level is best for a lactating sow?
quiz.explanation: Lactation rations should have 18% protein for high milk production.

quiz.q: What is a sign of mastitis in a lactating sow?
quiz.explanation: Mastitis causes the udder to become hard, hot, and painful.

quiz.q: Why should you provide creep feed to piglets from 2 weeks old?
options: A) To reduce demand on the sow
C) To stop them drinking milk
quiz.explanation: Creep feed reduces the sow's milk demand and helps piglets grow.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a sow is too fat using body condition scoring?
options: A) You can easily feel her bones
B) You cannot feel her bones even with firm pressure
C) She has a score of 2
quiz.explanation: A fat sow (score 4 or 5) has bones that are hard to feel.

quiz.q: What should you do if a sow scores 2 on body condition?
quiz.explanation: Increasing feed helps a thin sow gain condition.

quiz.q: How often should you body condition score your sows?
quiz.explanation: Monthly scoring helps you adjust feeding before problems arise.

quiz.q: What is the ideal body condition score for a sow at weaning?
quiz.explanation: Aim for score 3 at weaning so she can rebreed quickly.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to help with body condition scoring?
quiz.explanation: A picture chart with scores 1-5 helps you compare visually.

quiz.q: How many litters can a sow usually produce before culling?
quiz.explanation: Most sows stay productive for 6-8 litters.

quiz.q: Which of these is a reason to cull a sow?
options: A) She weans 20 piglets per year
B) She has repeated health problems
C) She is a good mother
quiz.explanation: Repeated health problems reduce productivity and profit.

quiz.q: What should you do before selling a cull sow?
options: A) Ensure she is not pregnant
D) Keep her for another year
quiz.explanation: Selling a pregnant sow wastes a potential litter.

quiz.q: How many sows should you plan to cull each year?
quiz.explanation: Culling 20-25% of sows annually keeps the herd productive.

quiz.q: What is a replacement gilt?
options: A) A young female pig kept for breeding
quiz.explanation: A gilt is a young female pig that will replace a culled sow.

quiz.q: How many sows can one boar serve?
quiz.explanation: One boar can comfortably serve 10-15 sows.

quiz.q: What protein level should a boar ration have?
quiz.explanation: A boar needs 14% protein for good fertility and condition.

quiz.q: How much space does a boar need?
quiz.explanation: A boar needs at least 6 square metres for exercise and comfort.

quiz.q: Why should you bring the sow to the boar's pen for mating?
quiz.explanation: The boar is more confident in his own pen, reducing aggression.

quiz.q: How often can a mature boar be used for mating?
quiz.explanation: A mature boar can mate 4-5 times per week without losing fertility.

quiz.q: Why should you rotate boars every 2 years?
quiz.explanation: Rotating boars prevents inbreeding and keeps genetics healthy.
